Compliment

/KOM-pluh-ment/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Compliment means a polite expression of praise or admiration.

After the recital, a stranger offered the young pianist a sincere compliment on her phrasing.

Worked Example

'Your essay's opening paragraph hooked me instantly' — that is a compliment: specific, sincere praise aimed straight at the writer.

The remark is direct, genuine praise for something the writer did well — exactly what a compliment is. Note the spelling: this is praise (complIment), not completion (complEment).

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

praise: an expression of approval

commendation: formal praise for an achievement

tribute: words or an act showing admiration and respect

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

insult: a rude remark meant to offend

criticism: an expression of disapproval

Where it sits · how lavishly approval is expressed — nod → compliment → rave

nod vs. compliment: A nod of approval acknowledges good work without a word; a compliment puts the praise into words.

rave vs. compliment: A compliment praises one thing sincerely; a rave gushes on and on about everything.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — com-

Prefix — com-: together, completely

Root — pli-

Root — pli-: to fill (a spelling of Latin plere, arriving via Italian complimento)

Suffix — -ment

Suffix — -ment: result or process of

Put it together

Put it together: The very same Latin pieces as complement — com- + pli- (to fill) + -ment — but this word traveled through Italian complimento and Spanish cumplimiento, 'fulfilling the courtesies owed to someone.' A compliment 'fills' your social duty of polite praise, which is how one Latin word split into today's two spellings.

Use the root in a new word: plenty

Use the root in a new word: plenty: After the harvest, the cellar held plenty of apples and squash.

Root Check

Word Choice

Everyday, social — spelling trap

Don't confuse this with complement (to complete or perfect something by adding what was missing). Remember: I give a complIment — the I is for what I say to praise you; complEment with an E is about completing. Compliment can also be a verb ('She complimented the chef'), and 'complimentary' can even mean free of charge ('complimentary breakfast') — a different branch of the same courtesy sense.
